subject: english-language
title: Stretch: Power in Texts Adventure
welcome_lead: Stretch — analyse power encoded in headlines, manifestos and political speeches.
meta_desc: GCSE English Language stretch — synthetic personalisation, ideology, lexical choice as power.
final_note: You explored synthetic personalisation, ideology and how lexical choice carries power in real texts.

concepts.def: Mass texts addressing 'you' to fake intimacy
Assumption built INTO the way something is said
Softening language to reduce force or claim

walkthroughs.body_html:
Adverts saying 'You deserve the best' fake one-to-one intimacy with millions.

Fairclough called this synthetic personalisation.

High modality: 'We MUST act now' (forceful, certain).

Low modality: 'We might perhaps consider.' (cautious).

Modal verbs encode power.

'When are you going to start working harder?' presupposes you AREN'T working hard.

Powerful — and slippery.

mcqs.q: An advert saying 'Treat YOURSELF — you deserve it' uses:
options: Modality
Synthetic personalisation
Hedging
Inversion

mcqs.q: 'You MUST do this' has what kind of modality?
options: Low
High
Neutral
Hedged
A noun is always a person, place or thing.
Passive voice means writing in the past tense.
A noun is any word that starts with a capital letter.
By the word's grammatical function in a sentence — not its meaning. The same word can belong to different classes depending on use (e.g. 'run' as noun or verb).

mcqs.q: What is convergence in accommodation theory?
options: When a speaker adjusts their speech to be more similar to their interlocutor's — to express solidarity, gain approval or ease communication.
A noun is any word that starts with a capital letter.
Convergence means two languages merge into one new language.
Convergence is when two speakers start using identical accents permanently.

mcqs.q: Why might a writer choose the passive voice?
options: The passive voice is always grammatically wrong.
Passive voice means writing in the past tense.
Convergence means two languages merge into one new language.
To foreground the patient rather than the agent, omit the agent when unknown or unimportant, sound formal/scientific, or distance the writer from action.
